sections.title: Basic Concept of Embedded Figures
sections.content: Embedded Figures questions require you to identify smaller shapes hidden inside a larger figure. The figure is usually described in words, and you must mentally construct it. The goal is to carefully observe lines, angles, and intersections to detect simple shapes like triangles, rectangles, or squares.

sections.title: Understanding the Description of a Large Figure
sections.content: Example: A rectangle where both diagonals are drawn and a vertical line passes exactly through the center. Step 1: Visualize a rectangle. Step 2: Draw both diagonals mentally from corner to corner. Step 3: Add a vertical line through the midpoint. Step 4: Now observe how many triangles and smaller rectangles are formed.

sections.title: Common 2D Shapes to Identify
sections.content: At Level 1, common shapes include square, rectangle, right-angled triangle, isosceles triangle, and circle. Carefully check if the required number of sides and angles are formed by the given lines.

sections.title: Method to Find the Embedded Shape
sections.content: 1. Break the large figure into smaller parts mentally. 2. Count intersection points. 3. Check if three lines form a closed triangle. 4. Check if four straight lines form a square or rectangle.

sections.title: 2–3 Step Solved Example
sections.content: Question: A square has both diagonals drawn. Is a right-angled triangle embedded? Solution: Step 1: A square has 90-degree angles. Step 2: A diagonal divides the square into two triangles. Step 3: Each triangle contains a 90-degree angle. Therefore, a right-angled triangle is present.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Looking only at outer boundaries. 2. Ignoring diagonal lines. 3. Not considering tilted shapes. 4. Making assumptions without verifying angles.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Embedded Figures require careful visualization. Always construct the full figure mentally, observe intersections, and verify angles and side lengths before answering.

tricks.title: Break the Figure Rule
tricks.explanation: Divide the large figure mentally into smaller sections.
tricks.example: A rectangle with one diagonal forms two triangles.

tricks.title: Count Intersections
tricks.explanation: More intersection points usually mean more hidden shapes.
tricks.example: If two diagonals cross, four smaller triangles are formed.

tricks.title: Right Angle Check
tricks.explanation: If a 90-degree angle is visible, a right-angled triangle or rectangle may exist.
tricks.example: Each corner of a square is 90 degrees.

tricks.title: Diagonal Importance
tricks.example: A square with two diagonals creates 8 small triangles.

tricks.title: Look Beyond the Border
tricks.explanation: Do not focus only on the outer boundary.
tricks.example: An inner vertical line may form a smaller rectangle.

tricks.title: Tilted Shape Detection
tricks.explanation: Some shapes may be rotated inside the figure.
tricks.example: A square can appear like a diamond when tilted.

tricks.title: Three-Line Rule for Triangles
tricks.explanation: Check if three straight lines form a closed region.
tricks.example: Two sides and one diagonal can form a triangle.

tricks.title: Verify Before Answering
tricks.explanation: Always confirm side count and angle type before selecting an option.
tricks.example: A rectangle must have four right angles.
